newsitem.title: JORDAN: Japan-Jordan fertiliser plant completed next week.
newsitem.headline: Japan-Jordan fertiliser plant completed next week.

text.p: A joint Japanese-Jordanian project to produce ammonium phosphates and compound fertiliser will be officially commissioned next week, industry officials said on Sunday.
The $85 million plant, built by Japanese Shiyoda engineering company at a site close to Jordan's Red Sea port of Aqaba, has already begun experimental production this month.

Its production is expected to build up gradually over the next year to its maximum capacity of 300,000 tonnes of mixed fertilisers annually. It will consume 80,000 tonnes of phosphoric acid annually or the equivalent of 260,000 tonnes of raw phosphate.
The Nippon-Jordan Fertiliser Company is a joint venture with Jordan Phosphates Mines Company, Arab Potash and a Japanese consortium which owns 60 percent of the venture.
Another $170 million Jordanian-Indian joint venture to export 200,000 tonnes of phosphoric acid to a fertiliser complex in India is expected to come on stream later next month.

Jordan Phosphate Mines Company is trying to tap $100 million in a bond issue offered internationally to part finance an estimated $250 million project to finance the second stage expansion of the firm's major Shidiyah mine.
The company was prompted to proceed quickly on Shidiyah by higher world demand and demand which the new joint venture downstream fertiliser projects will generate.

The Shidiyah project will more than double production to around eight million tonnes by 1998 and to a target of 10 million tonnes by 2000. Its high grade phosphate makes it by far the lowest cost producer of Jordan's three operating mines. It holds one billion tonnes of Jordan's proven reserves of 1.5 billion tonnes.
The company is more than 80 percent owned by the state and 16.28 percent by Kuwait.
